scope_note: Research support only, not legal or regulatory advice. Device assumed: body-worn research prototype recording ECG (skin electrodes) and the heart's magnetic field (non-contact sensors), battery, wireless link, cloud storage; small US company; 16-week bench feasibility phase; no clinical use, no patients, no marketing. Intended use has not been decided, so several entries are marked 'depends on intended use (not determined)'.
how_verified: verified=true means the quote was read on 2026-11-19 on the cited primary page. Regulation text (eCFR), the Federal Register rules, FDA guidance PDFs, the FDA recognized-standards database, the FDA device databases and IEC webstore pages were downloaded and read as raw text. ISO catalogue pages, the FDA QMSR page, the FDA software-assurance page, the FDA cybersecurity FAQ page and the AWS page were read through a fetch tool that returns short quotes; those are marked in notes. Full standard texts (ISO/IEC) are paywalled and were NOT read; clause lists for standards come from catalogue abstracts, FDA documents or general knowledge and are flagged where not confirmed.

items.name: ISO 13485:2016 Medical devices - Quality management systems - Requirements for regulatory purposes
items.edition: Edition 3, published 2016-03; reviewed and confirmed 2025 (stage 90.93 dated 2025-10-31). No newer edition.
items.what_it_requires: A documented quality management system covering management responsibility, resources, product realization (including design and development, purchasing, production) and measurement and improvement. It is the standard the US regulation now incorporates by reference.
items.why: ISO confirms the 2016 edition is still current; it becomes a legal requirement in the US through 21 CFR 820.10(a) for manufacturers of finished devices.
items.source_quote: This publication was last reviewed and confirmed in 2025. Therefore this version remains current.
items.notes: Read through fetch tool (iso.org itself returned HTTP 403; committee.iso.org mirror of the same catalogue page was readable). Top-level clause titles are from general knowledge of the standard, not read on the page. The same catalogue page also showed an undated 90.99 life-cycle entry that was not explained.

items.name: ISO 13485:2016 Clause 7.3 Design and development (sub-clause outline)
items.what_it_requires: Plan the design work, record inputs (requirements) and outputs (specifications), hold reviews, verify outputs against inputs, validate against user needs and intended use, control transfer to production, control changes, and keep a design and development file per device type.
items.why: 21 CFR 820.10(c) makes Clause 7.3 mandatory for class II and III device manufacturers; FDA's preamble cites sub-clauses 7.3.3, 7.3.4, 7.3.5, 7.3.7 and 7.3.10 by number.
clauses: 7.3.9 Control of design and development changes
items.source_quote: Clause 7.3.10 requires the design and development file to contain or reference all the records necessary to establish compliance with design and development requirements
items.notes: PARTLY verified. Confirmed on the Federal Register final rule: 7.3.3 and 7.3.4 exist, 7.3.5 is design and development review, 7.3.7 is design and development validation, 7.3.10 is the design and development file. The full list of ten sub-clause numbers and titles was NOT read in the standard itself (ISO online preview returned HTTP 403); titles for 7.3.8, 7.3.9 and 7.3.10 were corroborated only by search snippets of secondary tables of contents. Check against a purchased copy before quoting.

items.name: FDA Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR), 21 CFR Part 820 as amended (89 FR 7496, Feb. 2, 2024)
items.what_it_requires: Manufacturers of finished devices must document a quality management system that complies with ISO 13485:2016 plus FDA-specific additions (820.10, 820.35 records, 820.45 labeling and packaging). It replaced the Quality System Regulation; FDA states the rule now specifically requires risk management and that the old QSIT inspection technique is no longer used.
items.why: 820.1(a) scopes the rule to 'finished devices intended for human use'; whether a bench feasibility prototype already falls inside is not decided by the text alone (see STD-05).
clauses: 820.10 Requirements for a quality management system
items.source_quote: This rule is effective February 2, 2026.
items.notes: Changes named in primary sources: incorporation by reference of ISO 13485:2016 (820.7(b)) and ISO 9000:2015 Clause 3; design history file concept replaced by the design and development file (Clause 7.3.10) and the medical device file; the explicit QS-regulation requirement for an independent reviewer at each design review is not carried over (preamble, Comment 46). FDA page https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/postmarket-requirements-devices/quality-management-system-regulation-qmsr (content current 02/02/2026, read through fetch tool) states the rule 'now specifically requires risk management' and that QSIT was replaced by Compliance Program 7382.850. Titles of 820.35 and 820.45 are from general knowledge; only their section numbers were seen in 820.7(b).

items.name: 21 CFR 820.10(c) Design and development (which devices must follow Clause 7.3)
items.what_it_requires: Manufacturers of class II, class III and listed class I devices (including class I devices automated with computer software) must comply with ISO 13485 Clause 7.3 and its sub-clauses.
items.why: Electrocardiographs and ambulatory ECG devices are class II (STD-08, STD-09), so design controls would bind a product of that type; the device class of this prototype is not determined.
clauses: 820.10(d) Devices that support or sustain life
items.source_quote: must comply with the requirements in Design and Development, Clause 7.3 and its Subclauses in ISO 13485
items.notes: Text read from the eCFR renderer API for title 21 part 820 section 820.10.

items.name: When design controls start: concept and feasibility work (FDA preamble to the 1996 Quality System Regulation, 61 FR 52602, comment 62)
items.edition: Federal Register 1996-10-07 (preamble to the regulation that the QMSR replaced)
items.what_it_requires: FDA said design controls were not intended to cover concept development and feasibility studies, but that once it is decided a design will be developed, a plan must be established.
items.why: This is the only primary statement found on the feasibility boundary. It belongs to the superseded regulation; no equivalent sentence was found in the QMSR preamble, so its present weight is not determined.
items.source_quote: The design control requirements are not intended to apply to the development of concepts and feasibility studies.
items.notes: The next sentence reads: 'However, once it is decided that a design will be developed, a plan must be established'. The date on which a feasibility program becomes 'a design that will be developed' is a company decision that should be recorded. The QMSR final rule text was searched for 'feasibility' and 'concept' with no relevant hit.

items.name: 21 CFR 812.1(a) Investigational device exemption: what an IDE exempts, and the design-control carve-out
items.edition: eCFR current text (section last amended 90 FR 55979, Dec. 4, 2025)
items.what_it_requires: An approved IDE, or one considered approved under 812.2(b), exempts the device from several requirements including good manufacturing practice, except the design and development requirements of 820.10(c) if applicable.
items.why: The rule text keeps design controls in force for investigational devices; historically this pointed to 820.30 and now points to 820.10(c).
items.source_quote: good manufacturing practice requirements under section 520(f) except for the requirements found in § 820.10(c), if applicable
items.notes: FDA QMSR page (read through fetch tool) says IDE devices 'are not exempt from design and development requirements under 21 CFR 820.10(c) of the QMSR.' FDA's older IDE overview page (content current 08/22/2024) still cites 21 CFR 820.30. 1996 preamble comment 65 explains the reasoning: 'Because some of the device design occurs during the IDE stage, it is logical that manufacturers who intend to commercially produce the device follow design control procedures.'

items.name: 21 CFR 870.2340 Electrocardiograph
items.what_it_requires: Defines the electrocardiograph device type and places it in class II. Product codes under this regulation in FDA's database: DPS (Electrocardiograph), MLC (Monitor, ST segment).
items.why: Classification follows intended use; no intended use has been set for the prototype.
items.source_quote: used to process the electrical signal transmitted through two or more electrocardiograph electrodes and to produce a visual display of the electrical signal produced by the heart
items.notes: Classification line reads 'Class II (performance standards).' DPS record in openFDA: class 2, 510(k) submission type, not GMP exempt, third-party review eligible.

items.name: 21 CFR 870.2800 Medical magnetic tape recorder (the regulation FDA uses for ambulatory ECG product codes)
items.what_it_requires: Defines a recorder of physiological signals as class II. FDA's product classification database lists ambulatory ECG under it: MWJ (Electrocardiograph, Ambulatory, Without Analysis), MLO (Electrocardiograph, Ambulatory, With Analysis Algorithm), DSH (Recorder, Magnetic Tape, Medical), MXC (implantable event recorder without arrhythmia detection).
items.why: A wearable ECG recorder with an ambulatory-monitoring intended use would point here; not decided for this prototype.
items.source_quote: A medical magnetic tape recorder is a device used to record and play back signals from, for example, physiological amplifiers, signal conditioners, or computers.
items.notes: Product codes read from openFDA device classification API (api.fda.gov/device/classification.json?search=regulation_number:870.2800). The section title does not contain the words 'ambulatory ECG'; the link is through the product codes.

items.name: 21 CFR 870.2360 Electrocardiograph electrode
items.what_it_requires: Defines the skin electrode as its own class II device type with a special-controls guidance; exempt from premarket notification subject to 870.9. Product codes DRX (Electrode, Electrocardiograph) and MLN (multi-function).
items.why: Relevant if the company makes its own electrodes rather than buying legally marketed ones.
items.source_quote: The device is exempt from the premarket notification procedures in subpart E of part 807 of this chapter subject to the limitations in § 870.9.
items.notes: Special control named in the rule: 'Class II Special Controls Guidance Document: Electrocardiograph Electrodes.' That guidance was not read.

items.name: Magnetocardiograph: FDA product classification and 510(k) database search
items.edition: openFDA device classification and 510(k) data, queried 2026-11-19
items.what_it_requires: No requirement by itself. The search shows there is no device type or product code named for magnetocardiography; magnetocardiography systems found in the 510(k) database were cleared under product code DPS (electrocardiograph, 21 CFR 870.2340).
items.why: Six clearances of magnetic heart-recording systems carry the electrocardiograph product code; this is a lead for a regulatory professional, not a statement that this prototype is equivalent to any of them.
items.source_quote: CMI MAGNETOCARDIOGRAPH
items.notes: Classification database: searches of device_name for magnetocardiograph, magnetocardiography, biomagnetic, magnetometer returned nothing (HTTP 404 = zero results). Only magnetic entry found: 21 CFR 882.1400 product codes OLY (Magnetoencephalograph) and OLX (source localization software), neurology panel. See classification_findings.mcg for the K numbers. The 510(k) summaries themselves were not opened.

items.name: 21 CFR 812.2(a) and (c): when the IDE regulation applies to a study
items.what_it_requires: Part 812 applies to all clinical investigations of devices to determine safety and effectiveness, unless one of the listed exemptions in 812.2(c) applies.
items.why: Bench tests with no human involved are not an 'investigation' as defined in 812.3(h) (which needs 'one or more subjects'). Whether recordings on people are made 'to determine safety or effectiveness' depends on the purpose of the recordings, which has not been decided.
items.source_quote: This part applies to all clinical investigations of devices to determine safety and effectiveness, except as provided in paragraph (c) of this section.
items.notes: 812.3(h): 'Investigation means a clinical investigation or research involving one or more subjects to determine the safety or effectiveness of a device.' 812.2(c)(3) exempts certain noninvasive 'diagnostic device' testing but is tied to labeling under 809.10(c) (an in vitro diagnostic labeling rule); whether it can cover a non-IVD recorder was not determined here.

items.name: 21 CFR 812.2(b)(1): non-significant-risk route (abbreviated requirements)
items.what_it_requires: A study of a device that is not a significant risk device is considered to have an approved IDE without an application to FDA if the sponsor labels the device per 812.5, obtains and keeps IRB approval, ensures informed consent under part 50, monitors, keeps specified records and reports, and does not promote the device.
items.why: If recordings on people count as a device investigation and the device is non-significant risk, these seven conditions are the minimum; an IRB is still required.
items.source_quote: Obtains IRB approval of the investigation after presenting the reviewing IRB with a brief explanation of why the device is not a significant risk device, and maintains such approval
items.notes: Required label text under 812.5(a): 'CAUTION-Investigational device. Limited by Federal (or United States) law to investigational use.' (punctuation as in the rule is an em dash after CAUTION).

items.name: 21 CFR 812.3(m): definition of significant risk device
items.what_it_requires: Defines a significant risk device as an investigational device that is an implant, supports or sustains life, is of substantial importance in diagnosing or treating disease, or otherwise presents a potential for serious risk to a subject. A significant risk study needs an FDA-approved IDE (812.20(a)).
items.why: The significant / non-significant call is study-specific and is reviewed by an IRB; it has not been made for this device.
items.source_quote: Otherwise presents a potential for serious risk to the health, safety, or welfare of a subject.
items.notes: 812.3(m)(3) reads: 'Is for a use of substantial importance in diagnosing, curing, mitigating, or treating disease, or otherwise preventing impairment of human health and presents a potential for serious risk to the health, safety, or welfare of a subject'.

items.name: FDA Information Sheet: Significant Risk and Nonsignificant Risk Medical Device Studies (for IRBs, clinical investigators and sponsors)
items.what_it_requires: Explains that the sponsor makes the first risk call, the IRB reviews it and may change it, and FDA's determination is final where it has made one. A non-significant-risk study may start after IRB approval without an IDE application to FDA.
items.why: Shows that even the lightest FDA route for a device study on people runs through an IRB.
clauses: III.C Who decides whether a device study is SR or NSR
III.D Major differences between SR and NSR device studies
IV.A Sponsor responsibilities for NSR studies
items.source_quote: Sponsors are responsible for making the initial risk determination and presenting it to the IRB.
items.notes: Also in the sheet: 'NSR device studies do not have to have an IDE application approved by FDA.' The document was searched for 'employee', 'self' and 'themselves' with no match, and for ECG / electrocardio with no match.

items.name: Self-experimentation by engineers or investigators: position in primary sources
items.what_it_requires: No FDA or HHS primary document addressing self-experimentation by name was found. The definitions of 'subject' / 'human subject' contain no exception for the investigator or for company employees, and a subject may be a healthy person.
items.why: The regulations define subjects by what is done (a device is used on them in an investigation), not by who they are; whether engineers recording themselves are 'subjects' in an 'investigation' turns on the purpose of the recordings.
items.source_quote: A subject may be in normal health or may have a medical condition or disease.
items.notes: The quote is verified; the absence of a self-experimentation rule is a negative search result, not a quoted statement. 812.3(n) says a company that 'uses one or more of its own employees to conduct an investigation that it has initiated is a sponsor' and the employees are investigators; it says nothing about employees as subjects. University IRB policies found by search (secondary) generally treat self-experimenters as human subjects and require IRB review; one states the federal regulations are silent. Put this question to an IRB or regulatory professional.

items.name: 21 CFR 50.3 Definitions (FDA protection of human subjects)
items.what_it_requires: Defines clinical investigation (an experiment with a test article and one or more human subjects that must be submitted to FDA or whose results are intended to be submitted to or held for inspection by FDA), human subject, investigator, sponsor and test article. Part 50 sets informed consent rules for such investigations.
items.why: Applies if human recordings are a clinical investigation as defined, including when the results are intended to support a later FDA submission.
items.source_quote: Human subject means an individual who is or becomes a participant in research, either as a recipient of the test article or as a control.
items.notes: 50.3(c) includes experiments 'the results of which are intended to be submitted later to, or held for inspection by, the Food and Drug Administration as part of an application for a research or marketing permit.' 50.3(j): test article includes a 'medical device for human use'.

items.name: 21 CFR 56.102 and 56.103 (FDA institutional review boards)
items.what_it_requires: Defines clinical investigation, human subject, IRB and minimal risk in the same terms as part 50, and requires IRB review and approval before a clinical investigation that needs prior submission to FDA starts. FDA may refuse to consider data from a clinical investigation that had no IRB review.
items.why: 56.103(b) matters for planning: human data gathered without IRB review may be rejected in a later marketing application.
items.source_quote: shall not be initiated unless that investigation has been reviewed and approved by, and remains subject to continuing review by, an IRB meeting the requirements of this part
items.notes: 56.102(e): 'Human subject means an individual who is or becomes a participant in research, either as a recipient of the test article or as a control. A subject may be either a healthy individual or a patient.' 56.103(b): FDA 'may decide not to consider in support of an application for a research or marketing permit any data' from an investigation not approved by an IRB.

items.name: 45 CFR 46.102 and 46.101 (Common Rule): human subject, research, and scope
items.what_it_requires: Defines research as a systematic investigation designed to develop or contribute to generalizable knowledge, and a human subject as a living individual about whom an investigator obtains information through intervention or interaction, or identifiable private information. The policy applies to research conducted, supported or otherwise regulated by a federal department or agency that has adopted it.
items.why: 46.101(a) ties the Common Rule to federal conduct, support or regulation; privately funded recordings may fall outside it, while federally funded work (for example under a federal grant) would bring it in.
clauses: 46.101(a) To what does this policy apply
items.source_quote: Research means a systematic investigation, including research development, testing, and evaluation, designed to develop or contribute to generalizable knowledge.
items.notes: 46.102(e)(1)(i): a human subject is 'a living individual about whom an investigator (whether professional or student) conducting research: (i) Obtains information or biospecimens through intervention or interaction with the individual, and uses, studies, or analyzes the information or biospecimens'. Recording a physiological signal from a volunteer is an interaction; whether the activity is 'research' as defined depends on its design and purpose. State human-research laws and any funder terms were not researched.

items.name: ISO 14971:2019 Medical devices - Application of risk management to medical devices
items.edition: Edition 3, 2019-12; reviewed and confirmed 2025 (stage 90.93 dated 2025-03-07). FDA recognition number 5-125 (complete).
items.what_it_requires: A documented process to identify hazards, estimate and evaluate risks, control them, judge overall residual risk, review the result, and keep monitoring after production. It applies across the whole life cycle and does not set acceptable risk levels.
items.why: It applies to 'all stages of the life-cycle', and FDA states the QMSR now specifically requires risk management; starting the risk file during feasibility avoids rebuilding it later.
clauses: 4 General requirements for risk management system
items.source_quote: The requirements of this International Standard are applicable to all stages of the life-cycle of a medical device.
items.notes: Edition and scope read on FDA's recognized consensus standards database; ISO status read through fetch tool at https://committee.iso.org/standard/72704.html. Clause titles are from general knowledge of the standard (FDA's page confirms clauses 5.5, 6 and 7 exist) and were not read in the standard text. FDA's entry notes that the probability-based risk model does not carry over to cybersecurity risk.

items.name: ISO/TR 24971:2020 Medical devices - Guidance on the application of ISO 14971
items.what_it_requires: Non-mandatory guidance on setting up and running the ISO 14971 process (risk acceptability criteria, hazard identification aids, risk control options, production and post-production information).
items.why: It is a technical report (guidance), listed by FDA as a supportive publication for ISO 14971, not a requirement in itself.
items.source_quote: non-mandatory guidance on the development, implementation, and maintenance of a risk management system for medical devices
items.notes: Read through fetch tool; the quote is from the catalogue page's overview section as returned by the tool. A revision has been started (stage 90.92); no publication date for the revision was found.

items.name: IEC 62304:2006+AMD1:2015 Medical device software - Software life cycle processes
items.edition: Edition 1.1 consolidated (2015-06-26); stability date 2028; a second edition is under development (IEC webstore stage shown: 'Approved for CD'). FDA recognition number 13-79 (complete).
items.what_it_requires: Life-cycle processes for medical device software: development planning, requirements, architecture, detailed design, unit and integration testing, system testing, release, maintenance, risk management, configuration management and problem resolution, scaled by software safety class A, B or C.
items.why: Applies to software that is a medical device or embedded in one; the prototype firmware and cloud code are not yet medical device software in a regulatory sense, but FDA accepts a declaration of conformity to this standard in premarket submissions.
items.source_quote: This standard does not cover validation and final release of the medical device, even when the medical device consists entirely of software.
items.notes: Edition, stability date and development stage read on the IEC webstore page; the same abstract is on FDA's recognition page. Safety classes (A: no injury possible or risk acceptable; B: non-serious injury possible; C: death or serious injury possible) and clause titles were NOT read in the standard text; FDA's software guidance confirms clause 6 (maintenance) and clause 8 (configuration management). Publication timing of edition 2 could not be confirmed: secondary sources disagree (2027 to 2029) and report that it would replace classes A/B/C with two rigor levels.

items.name: FDA guidance: Content of Premarket Submissions for Device Software Functions
items.edition: Final, issued June 14, 2023 (supersedes the May 2005 software guidance)
items.what_it_requires: Sets the software documentation FDA recommends in a premarket submission at one of two levels, Basic or Enhanced, chosen by the risk of the software function in the device's intended use. For development and maintenance practices it accepts a declaration of conformity to the FDA-recognized version of IEC 62304 as an alternative to submitting the plans.
items.why: It governs submission content, so it binds at the marketing-submission stage; it shapes what records the software work should already be producing.
clauses: Software Development, Configuration Management, and Maintenance Practices
Software Testing as part of Verification and Validation
items.source_quote: The Documentation Level of a device is based on the risks of its device software function(s) in the context of the device's intended use
items.notes: Guidance is nonbinding ('Contains Nonbinding Recommendations'). Landing page: https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/content-premarket-submissions-device-software-functions. The guidance uses its own two documentation levels; it does not map them to IEC 62304 classes A/B/C.

items.name: FDA guidance: Computer Software Assurance for Production and Quality Management System Software
items.edition: Final, February 2026; supersedes the final guidance 'Computer Software Assurance for Production and Quality System Software' issued September 24, 2025. Docket FDA-2022-D-0795.
items.what_it_requires: A risk-based approach to assuring software used in device production or in the quality management system (not software in the device itself).
items.why: It concerns production and quality-system software of a device manufacturer; a bench feasibility phase has neither a production line nor a regulated quality system. It becomes relevant when such tools are used under the QMSR.
items.source_quote: FDA is issuing this guidance to provide recommendations on computer software assurance
items.notes: Read through fetch tool (status, date and superseded document as stated on the FDA page). The guidance PDF itself was not opened. The older URL ending 'quality-system-software' now returns HTTP 404.

items.name: IEC 62366-1:2015+AMD1:2020 Medical devices - Part 1: Application of usability engineering to medical devices
items.what_it_requires: A usability (human factors) engineering process to analyse, specify, develop and evaluate the usability of a device as it relates to safety, covering risks from correct use and use error in normal use. It can identify, but does not assess or mitigate, risks from abnormal use; IEC 62366-2 gives guidance.
items.why: It is written for a manufacturer's device development process; nothing in the sources binds it to a bench prototype, but use-related hazards (electrode placement, wearing position) feed the risk file.
items.source_quote: specifies a PROCESS for a MANUFACTURER to analyse, specify, develop and evaluate the USABILITY of a MEDICAL DEVICE as it relates to SAFETY
items.notes: Edition and scope read on FDA's recognized-standards database. The IEC catalogue page was not separately read, so a newer IEC edition after 2020 was not ruled out on IEC's own site. Related FDA guidance listed there: 'Applying Human Factors and Usability Engineering to Medical Devices', issued February 3, 2016.

items.name: IEC 60601-1:2005+AMD1:2012+AMD2:2020 Medical electrical equipment - Part 1: General requirements for basic safety and essential performance
items.edition: Edition 3.2 consolidated, 2020-08-20; stability date 2028. FDA recognition number 19-49 (with US national differences, ANSI/AAMI ES60601-1).
items.what_it_requires: General safety requirements for medical electrical equipment: protection against electric shock (including patient leakage current limits and applied-part classification), mechanical, thermal and other hazards, plus essential performance, tied to a risk management process.
items.why: It applies to medical electrical equipment; a research prototype is not yet that, but its electrode-to-skin connection is exactly the hazard the standard addresses, so its leakage and isolation limits are the sensible design target before anyone is connected.
items.source_quote: This International Standard applies to the BASIC SAFETY and ESSENTIAL PERFORMANCE of MEDICAL ELECTRICAL EQUIPMENT and MEDICAL ELECTRICAL SYSTEMS
items.notes: Edition and stability date also read on the IEC webstore (https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/67497). FDA accepts a declaration of conformity 'when the US national differences are applied'. Clause numbers are not listed because the standard text was not read.

items.name: IEC 60601-1-2:2014+AMD1:2020 Collateral standard: Electromagnetic disturbances - Requirements and tests
items.what_it_requires: Emission limits and immunity tests for medical electrical equipment so that basic safety and essential performance hold in the presence of electromagnetic disturbances, with test levels set by the intended use environment.
items.why: It applies to medical electrical equipment; for a prototype, pre-compliance checks against it are a design aid, not an obligation found in the sources.
items.source_quote: BASIC SAFETY with regard to ELECTROMAGNETIC DISTURBANCES is applicable to all ME EQUIPMENT and ME SYSTEMS.
items.notes: FDA does not recognize two parts (the 'nursing homes' example in Figure 3 and Note k of Table 8). Related FDA guidance listed: 'Electromagnetic Compatibility (EMC) of Medical Devices', issued July 6, 2022, and 'Radio Frequency Wireless Technology in Medical Devices', issued August 13, 2013 (neither opened). IEC catalogue page for this standard not separately read.

items.name: IEC 60601-1-11:2015+AMD1:2020 Collateral standard: Requirements for medical electrical equipment and systems used in the home healthcare environment
items.what_it_requires: Extra requirements (environmental ranges, ingress protection, lay-operator instructions and similar) for equipment the manufacturer intends for use in the home healthcare environment, whether operated by lay people or trained staff.
items.why: It applies only if the manufacturer specifies home healthcare use in the instructions for use; a body-worn device used outside clinics would normally be in scope, but the use environment has not been declared.
items.source_quote: applies regardless of whether the ME EQUIPMENT or ME SYSTEM is intended for use by a LAY OPERATOR or by trained healthcare personnel
items.notes: FDA does not recognize 'Note 2 to entry' in sub-clause 3.1. IEC catalogue page not separately read.

items.name: IEC 60601-2-25:2011 Particular requirements for the basic safety and essential performance of electrocardiographs
items.edition: Edition 2.0, 2011-10-19; stability date 2026. FDA recognition number 3-105 (partial).
items.what_it_requires: Safety and performance requirements for electrocardiographs that produce ECG reports for diagnostic purposes. Ambulatory ECG equipment and cardiac monitors are excluded where they are not intended for diagnostic ECG reports.
items.why: Scope is defined by a diagnostic-report intended use, which has not been decided.
items.source_quote: electrocardiographs intended by themselves or as a part of a medical electrical system, for the production of electrocardiogram reports for diagnostic purposes
items.notes: FDA's entry lists four sub-clauses it does not recognize (201.12.1.101.2, 201.12.1.101.3.1, 201.12.1.101.3.2, 202.6.2.6.1 bb). A replacement project exists (see STD-31).

items.name: IEC 60601-2-27:2011 Particular requirements for the basic safety and essential performance of electrocardiographic monitoring equipment
items.edition: Edition 3.0, 2011-03-30 (with Corrigendum 1:2012); stability date 2026. FDA recognition number 3-126 (partial).
items.what_it_requires: Safety and performance requirements for ECG monitoring equipment used in hospitals and in settings such as ambulances and air transport. FDA's abstract states that ambulatory (Holter) monitors and home-use ECG monitors are outside its scope.
items.why: It targets hospital-type patient monitoring; a body-worn recorder is more likely to fall under IEC 60601-2-47, but that depends on the intended use.
items.source_quote: applies to electrocardiographic monitoring equipments used in a hospital environment as well as when used outside the hospital environment, such as in ambulances and air transport
items.notes: FDA abstract (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfStandards/detail.cfm?standard__identification_no=44850): 'Ambulatory ("Holter") monitors, fetal heart rate monitors, pulse plethysmographic devices, and other ECG recording equipment are outside the scope of this particular standard.' The IEC abstract says the standard also applies to hospital ECG telemetry while the FDA abstract says it is not applicable to ECG telemetry systems; the two summaries differ and the standard text was not read.

items.name: IEC 60601-2-47:2012 Particular requirements for the basic safety and essential performance of ambulatory electrocardiographic systems
items.edition: Edition 2.0, 2012-02-16; stability date 2026. FDA recognition number 3-155 (complete).
items.what_it_requires: Safety and performance requirements for ambulatory ECG systems that record continuously and analyse the ECG (full or partial recording). FDA links it to product codes MLO (ambulatory ECG with analysis) and MWI.
items.why: The closest particular standard for a body-worn ECG recorder, but in scope only for systems of the listed types; not determined for this prototype.
items.source_quote: IEC 60601-2-47:2012 concerns the basic safety and essential performance of AMBULATORY ELECTROCARDIOGRAPHIC SYSTEMS.
items.notes: Webstore abstract continues: 'It amends and supplements the general standard IEC 60601-1 (third edition 2005).' A search snippet of the same page reports that intermittent event recorders are excluded; that sentence was not read directly. No particular standard for magnetocardiographs was found in FDA's recognized-standards database or in the searches run.

items.name: IEC/DIS 80601-2-86 Particular requirements for electrocardiographs, including diagnostic equipment, monitoring equipment, ambulatory equipment, electrodes, cables and leadwires
items.edition: Under development: Draft International Standard, edition 1, stage 40.60 (close of voting) dated 2026-10-03. Not published.
items.what_it_requires: A single future particular standard for ECG equipment across diagnostic, monitoring and ambulatory use, including electrodes and cables.
items.why: It is a draft; no obligation attaches to an unpublished standard. It matters for a product that will be tested one to three years from now.
items.source_quote: Medical electrical equipment — Part 2-86: Particular requirements for the basic safety
items.notes: Read through fetch tool. The catalogue page does not say which standards it will replace; a secondary article says the project combines the three current IEC ECG particular standards, which matches IEC 60601-2-25, -2-27 and -2-47 but was not confirmed on a primary page. FDA's recognized-standards search for 80601-2-86 returned nothing.

items.name: Applied-part classification for ECG electrodes (type BF / type CF, defibrillation-proof)
items.edition: IEC 60601-1 Ed. 3.2 and the ECG particular standards (texts not read)
items.what_it_requires: IEC 60601-1 classifies parts that touch the patient as type B, BF or CF applied parts, with CF the most stringent leakage-current class; the ECG particular standards set which type an ECG applied part must be.
items.why: No primary or standards-body summary stating the required type was found; the requirement sits in paywalled standard text.
items.notes: NOT VERIFIED. A third-party guide to IEC 60601-2-25:2011 states that under sub-clause 201.6.2 'the ECG applied part must now be Type CF'; a practitioner forum thread shows disagreement about BF versus CF for skin-electrode devices. Nothing was found for IEC 60601-2-47. Read the purchased standards or ask a test laboratory before fixing the isolation design target; designing to the CF limit is the conservative choice (judgement, not sourced).

items.name: ISO 10993-1:2025 Biological evaluation of medical devices - Part 1: Requirements and general principles for the evaluation of biological safety within a risk management process
items.edition: Sixth edition, 2025-11 (published; replaces the fifth edition 2018-08). FDA recognition number 2-313, entered 05/25/2026, partial; declarations to the 2018 edition accepted until July 1, 2029.
items.what_it_requires: A biological evaluation, inside the ISO 14971 risk process, of devices that contact the body directly or indirectly: characterize materials and contact, use existing data, identify gaps, test only where needed. The scope says the principles can be applied to prototype or development-stage devices.
items.why: The standard's own scope calls a biological evaluation 'a pre-requisite for conducting a clinical trial'; whether recordings on engineers are a clinical trial is not determined, but skin-contact materials should be chosen with this in mind now.
clauses: 6.5.11.3 (FDA does not recognize the phrase 'consumer products')
6.9 Biological risk estimation (not recognized by FDA)
items.source_quote: For example, a biological evaluation is a pre-requisite for conducting a clinical trial.
items.notes: Edition and scope read on FDA's recognized-standards database (quoting the standard's abstract). The ISO catalogue page for the 2025 edition was not read. How the 2025 edition words its contact and duration categories was NOT read; the categories in STD-34 are those of the 2018 edition as used in FDA's 2023 guidance. FDA notes the 2025 genotoxicity requirements 'may not align' with its guidance for prolonged-contact devices and asks sponsors to contact the review offices.

items.name: FDA guidance: Use of International Standard ISO 10993-1, 'Biological evaluation of medical devices - Part 1: Evaluation and testing within a risk management process'
items.edition: Final, issued September 8, 2023 (supersedes the September 4, 2020 version); written against ISO 10993-1:2018
items.what_it_requires: Categorizes devices by nature of body contact and contact duration: A limited (24 hours or less), B prolonged (more than 24 hours to 30 days), C long term (more than 30 days). For a surface device on intact skin, Table A.1 marks three endpoints at every duration: cytotoxicity, sensitization, and irritation or intracutaneous reactivity. Attachment G allows a reduced submission for intact-skin devices made from listed common polymers and fabrics.
items.why: It is premarket-submission guidance (it also names IDEs). A skin electrode and a chest-worn housing are surface devices contacting intact skin; the duration category depends on the intended wear time, which is not determined.
clauses: Attachment A, Table A.1 Biocompatibility Evaluation Endpoints
Attachment G Biocompatibility of Certain Devices in Contact with Intact Skin
items.source_quote: Medical devices or components that contact intact skin surfaces only, as described in section 5.2.2 (a) of ISO 10993-1:2018
items.notes: Guidance is nonbinding. Attachment G lists situations needing extra discussion, including devices 'indicated for use in pregnant women' and for neonates. The list of included materials (Attachment G section B) and exclusions (section C) was not transcribed; conductive gels and adhesives of electrodes should be checked against it. Buying legally marketed ECG electrodes instead of making them moves the electrode biocompatibility question to the supplier (judgement, not sourced).

items.name: IEC 62133-2:2017+AMD1:2021 Safety requirements for portable sealed secondary lithium cells and batteries, for use in portable applications - Part 2: Lithium systems
items.edition: Edition 1.1 consolidated, 2021-07. FDA recognition number 19-55 (complete), entered 05/26/2025; declarations to Edition 1.0 accepted until July 2, 2028.
items.what_it_requires: Requirements and tests for safe operation of portable rechargeable lithium cells and batteries under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse.
items.why: No source makes it mandatory for a bench prototype; FDA recognizes it for device submissions, so choosing cells and packs that already hold a test report to it costs little now.
items.source_quote: specifies requirements and tests for the safe operation of portable sealed secondary lithium cells and batteries containing non-acid electrolyte, under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse
items.notes: FDA's transition paragraph on this page calls the new recognition 'IEC 62133-2 Edition 5.0 2021-09', which conflicts with the heading 'Edition 1.1 2021-07' on the same page; treated here as an error in the transition text. IEC catalogue page not separately read.

items.name: UN Manual of Tests and Criteria, sub-section 38.3 (lithium battery transport tests), as required by 49 CFR 173.185
items.edition: 49 CFR 173.185, eCFR current text (the UN Manual itself was not read)
items.what_it_requires: Every lithium cell or battery offered for transport must be of a type proven to pass the UN 38.3 tests, and manufacturers must keep a test record. Paragraph (e) excepts prototypes transported for testing and production runs of up to 100 per year from the testing and record-keeping, under special packaging conditions.
items.why: It binds anyone who ships lithium cells, batteries or equipment containing them, including a prototype sent to a test laboratory or partner; it does not depend on the device being medical.
clauses: 49 CFR 173.185(e) Low production runs and prototypes
items.source_quote: Each lithium cell or battery must be of the type proven to meet the criteria in part III, sub-section 38.3 of the UN Manual of Tests and Criteria
items.notes: 'Applies now' only when batteries are actually shipped; buying cells and packs that already have a UN 38.3 test summary from the supplier is the usual route (judgement, not sourced). 173.185(e): 'prototype lithium cells or batteries transported for purposes of testing, and equipment containing such cells or batteries are excepted from the testing and record keeping requirements of paragraph (a)' subject to conditions. Air-transport (ICAO/IATA) rules were not researched. The UNECE page for the Manual returned HTTP 403.

items.name: FCC 47 CFR 15.201(b): certification of intentional radiators
items.what_it_requires: An intentional radiator operating under Part 15 (for example a Bluetooth or Wi-Fi transmitter) must be certified through a Telecommunication Certification Body before it is marketed. 47 CFR 2.803(b) bars marketing a radio-frequency device without valid authorization.
items.why: The certification duty is tied to marketing; no marketing happens in this phase.
items.source_quote: shall be certified by the Telecommunication Certification Bodies pursuant to the procedures in subpart J of part 2 of this chapter prior to marketing
items.notes: 15.23 (home-built devices: 'not marketed, are not constructed from a kit, and are built in quantities of five or less for personal use') was read but whether a company's prototypes are 'for personal use' is not determined.

items.name: FCC 47 CFR 15.212: modular transmitters (use of a pre-certified radio module)
items.what_it_requires: Sets the conditions under which a self-contained radio module gets its own approval (own shielding, buffered data inputs, own power regulation, approved antenna and so on), so that a host product can incorporate it.
items.why: Designing around a module that already holds a modular grant, with its approved antenna, keeps the later product authorization small; the host-product conditions were not read in an FCC guidance document.
items.source_quote: Single modular transmitters consist of a completely self-contained radiofrequency transmitter device that is typically incorporated into another product, host or device.
items.notes: What the host product still has to be tested for (unintentional emissions, any change of antenna, co-located transmitters, RF exposure for a body-worn device) is set out in FCC guidance (KDB publications) that was not read.

items.name: FCC 47 CFR 2.805: operating a radio-frequency device before equipment authorization
items.what_it_requires: A radio-frequency device may not be operated before authorization unless a listed condition is met: an experimental licence, operation fully inside an anechoic chamber or Faraday cage, or, for Part 15 devices, operation in compliance with the technical rules for purposes that include evaluation during development.
items.why: This is the rule that covers switching on a prototype radio during development; using an already certified module unmodified with its approved antenna is the simplest way to stay inside the technical rules.
items.source_quote: Evaluation of performance and determination of customer acceptability, during developmental, design, or pre-production states.
items.notes: 2.805(d) requires that devices are 'either rendered inoperable or retrieved at the conclusion of such operation', and adds labelling if the device is 'not operated at the manufacturer's facilities' (relevant to prototypes worn off-site).

items.name: Bluetooth Qualification Process (Bluetooth SIG)
items.edition: Bluetooth SIG qualification overview page, read 2026-11-19
items.what_it_requires: Any product using Bluetooth technology must be qualified by the company under its own SIG membership before it is sold or distributed; a supplier's module qualification does not transfer automatically.
items.why: The SIG ties the duty to selling or distributing the product, which does not happen in this phase.
items.source_quote: All Bluetooth products must complete the Bluetooth Qualification Process on or before the date that you begin to sell or distribute the product.
items.notes: Same page: 'Your supplier or other member companies cannot qualify your products on your behalf.' This is a licence-agreement obligation, not a government regulation. Fee amounts were not read.

items.name: FDA guidance: Cybersecurity in Medical Devices: Quality Management System Considerations and Content of Premarket Submissions
items.edition: Final, issued February 3, 2026; supersedes the June 27, 2025 guidance of nearly the same name ('Quality System Considerations'). Docket FDA-2021-D-1158.
items.what_it_requires: Recommends designing security in through a Secure Product Development Framework (threat modelling, security risk management, security architecture, testing) and lists the cybersecurity documentation for premarket submissions, including what cyber devices must provide under section 524B.
items.why: It addresses premarket submission content and quality-system practice; for a prototype it is a design reference, since retrofitting security architecture later is costly.
clauses: V Using an SPDF to Manage Cybersecurity Risks
items.source_quote: An SPDF is a set of processes that help identify and reduce the number and severity of vulnerabilities in products.
items.notes: The title in the request ('Quality System Considerations') is the superseded June 2025 title. Guidance is nonbinding except where it restates section 524B. Landing page: https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/cybersecurity-medical-devices-quality-management-system-considerations-and-content-premarket.

items.name: Section 524B of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 360n-2), 'cyber device'
items.what_it_requires: The sponsor of a 510(k), PMA, PDP, De Novo or HDE for a cyber device must submit a plan to monitor and address postmarket vulnerabilities, maintain processes giving reasonable assurance the device and related systems are cybersecure (including patches), and provide a software bill of materials.
items.why: It attaches to premarket submissions. A device with sponsor-authorized software that can connect to the internet, as a cloud-connected wearable would, meets the three-part definition on its face; confirm with a regulatory professional.
items.source_quote: includes software validated, installed, or authorized by the sponsor as a device or in a device; (2) has the ability to connect to the internet
items.notes: Definition quoted from FDA's guidance, which quotes the statute; statute text also read through fetch tool at law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/21/360n-2 (the uscode.house.gov link returned HTTP 404). Effective date and submission types from FDA's FAQ page https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/medical-device-cybersecurity/cybersecurity-resources-medical-device-manufacturers-guidance-resources-and-faqs (read through fetch tool: 'This authority took effect on March 29, 2023.').

items.name: IEC 81001-5-1:2021 Health software and health IT systems safety, effectiveness and security - Part 5-1: Security - Activities in the product life cycle
items.what_it_requires: Life-cycle requirements for developing and maintaining health software securely, aligned to IEC 62443-4-1. FDA's guidance names it as one possible secure product development framework.
items.why: FDA lists it among frameworks that 'may' satisfy its recommendations and warns that conformance alone may not meet section 524B.
items.source_quote: Conformance to this standard may not satisfy all the cybersecurity requirements outlined in Section 524B of FD&C Act
items.notes: FDA's guidance also names the Medical Device and Health IT Joint Security Plan (JSP2) and ANSI/ISA 62443-4-1 as frameworks. IEC catalogue page not separately read.

items.name: HIPAA: covered entity and business associate (45 CFR 160.103)
items.what_it_requires: HIPAA duties fall on covered entities (health plans, health care clearinghouses, and health care providers who transmit health information electronically in connection with a covered transaction) and on business associates that create, receive, maintain or transmit protected health information on behalf of a covered entity.
items.why: Applicability turns on who the company is and for whom it holds data, not on the data being about health; a developer recording non-patients for its own research does not appear in either definition, but that conclusion is for counsel.
items.source_quote: A health care provider who transmits any health information in electronic form in connection with a transaction covered by this subchapter.
items.notes: Business associate definition begins: 'business associate means, with respect to a covered entity, a person who: (i) On behalf of such covered entity ... creates, receives, maintains, or transmits protected health information'. HIPAA would become relevant if the company later receives patient data from, or works on behalf of, a hospital, clinic or insurer.

items.name: HHS/NIH statement that health information held by a non-covered entity is outside the Privacy Rule but may have other protections
items.edition: NIH 'HIPAA Privacy Rule and research' pages (date not confirmed; reported as old)
items.what_it_requires: States that the Privacy Rule protects information held by covered entities, that researchers are not themselves covered entities unless they are also providers conducting covered electronic transactions, and that other federal and state protections may still cover the information.
items.why: Supports the reading that research data from non-patients held by a device developer may sit outside HIPAA while other obligations remain.
items.source_quote: is not protected by the Privacy Rule
items.notes: NOT VERIFIED on the page: the NIH site refused connections and hhs.gov returned HTTP 403 on 2026-11-19. The wording comes from a search-engine extract: 'individually identifiable health information that is held by anyone other than a covered entity, including an independent researcher who is not a covered entity, is not protected by the Privacy Rule', followed by a remark that other Federal and State protections may cover the information. Other obligations NOT researched here: FTC Act and the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule, state consumer-health-data and privacy laws, contract and consent terms, and funder data rules.

items.name: AWS: Business Associate Addendum and HIPAA-eligible services
items.what_it_requires: Where HIPAA applies, AWS requires a signed Business Associate Addendum for the account, and protected health information may be processed, stored and transmitted only in services on the HIPAA-eligible list.
items.why: Needed before any ePHI goes to AWS; if the stored recordings are not PHI (see STD-44) the BAA is not triggered, though choosing eligible services from the start avoids a later migration.
items.source_quote: they should only process, store, and transmit protected health information (PHI) in the HIPAA-eligible services
items.notes: Read through fetch tool. Same page describes the BAA as 'an AWS contract that is required under HIPAA rules' and says customers 'may use any AWS service in an account designated as a HIPAA account'. The eligible-services list is at https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/hipaa-eligible-services-reference/ (not read).

mcg.finding: Nothing found in the FDA product classification database for device names containing magnetocardiograph, magnetocardiography, biomagnetic or magnetometer (zero results on 2026-11-19).

Only magnetic biosignal device type found: 21 CFR 882.1400 product codes OLY (Magnetoencephalograph) and OLX (Source Localization Software For Electroencephalograph Or Magnetoencephalograph), class II, neurology. This is brain, not heart.

mcg.note: Found by name pattern; device name does not itself say magnetocardiograph and the 510(k) summary was not opened.
Cleared under the electrocardiograph code; summary not opened.
Found by applicant search; summary not opened.
Found by device name 'MCG' within product code DPS; summary not opened.

classification_findings.notes: All 510(k) records come from the openFDA 510(k) API (api.fda.gov/device/510k.json) queried on 2026-11-19 with generic terms. The list is a set of leads, not a complete census: devices whose names do not contain magnet/MCG/biomagnet terms would be missed, and the 510(k) summaries (intended use, predicates, shielded-room versus unshielded use) were not read. None of these clearances implies that the prototype is equivalent to any of them. No De Novo or PMA search was run. FDA's database shows no product code or regulation specific to magnetocardiography; every heart-magnetic-field clearance found used the electrocardiograph code DPS.

open_questions_for_a_regulatory_professi: Are recordings made on the engineers themselves an 'investigation' under 21 CFR 812.3(h) and a 'clinical investigation' under 21 CFR 50.3(c) / 56.102(c)? If yes, which route applies: exempt, non-significant-risk with IRB approval (812.2(b)), or significant risk? No primary source on self-experimentation was found.
If any human recordings may later support a marketing submission, must they have IRB review now so FDA will consider the data (21 CFR 56.103(b))?

Does federal funding (for example a federal small-business research award) bring the Common Rule (45 CFR 46) and an IRB or exemption determination into play for any volunteer recordings, and what do the funder's own terms require?

At what documented point does the feasibility program become 'a design that will be developed', so that ISO 13485 Clause 7.3 / 21 CFR 820.10(c) design controls should start? Does the 1996 preamble position on feasibility still reflect FDA's view under the QMSR?

What intended use and indications would the product carry, and which classification follows: electrocardiograph (870.2340, DPS), ambulatory ECG (870.2800, MWJ/MLO), another code, or De Novo? Do the six magnetocardiography clearances under DPS offer a usable predicate for a body-worn, unshielded device?
Is the combined ECG-plus-magnetic device one device or two functions, and does adding the magnetic channel raise new questions of safety or effectiveness for a 510(k)?

Which applied-part type (BF or CF, defibrillation-proof or not) do IEC 60601-2-25 and IEC 60601-2-47 require for the electrode connection, and what patient leakage limits should the prototype meet before anyone is connected to it?
Should product testing target the current ECG particular standards (IEC 60601-2-25/-27/-47, stability date 2026) or the draft IEC 80601-2-86, given the likely test date?
Does the 21 CFR 812.2(c)(3) diagnostic-device exemption have any application to a noninvasive recorder that is not an in vitro diagnostic?

Which contact-duration category (limited, prolonged, long term, counted cumulatively) applies to the electrodes and housing under ISO 10993-1:2025, and do the chosen materials qualify for FDA's Attachment G intact-skin policy? Is use during pregnancy intended (Attachment G flags it)?

Do recordings from employees and volunteers trigger any privacy duties outside HIPAA: FTC Health Breach Notification Rule, state consumer health data laws, employment law on employee health data, and consent and retention terms?
Is the company a HIPAA business associate at any point (for example if a clinic partner supplies patient data), which would require an AWS Business Associate Addendum before upload?

For the radio: does operating prototypes worn outside the company's premises fit 47 CFR 2.805(d), and what host-level FCC testing and RF-exposure evaluation remain when a pre-certified module is used in a body-worn product?
For lithium batteries: do planned prototype shipments rely on supplier UN 38.3 test summaries or on the 49 CFR 173.185(e) prototype exception, and what do carrier and air-transport rules add?
not_found: No primary FDA or HHS/OHRP statement specifically about self-experimentation by investigators or engineers. Only university IRB policies (secondary) were found.
No FDA product code, classification regulation or recognized consensus standard specific to magnetocardiographs.
The full list of ISO 13485:2016 Clause 7.3 sub-clause titles on a primary page (ISO preview blocked); see STD-02.
Primary or standards-body text stating the required applied-part type (BF/CF) for ECG electrodes; see STD-32.
IEC 62304 software safety class definitions in the standard text (paywalled); publication date of IEC 62304 edition 2.
The wording of contact and duration categories in ISO 10993-1:2025 (only the 2018-based FDA guidance categories were read).
A readable HHS page on HIPAA covered entities or on research data held by non-covered entities (hhs.gov returned HTTP 403; NIH site refused connections).
IMDRF documents (imdrf.org timed out or reset the connection); no IMDRF source is cited in this file.
The UN Manual of Tests and Criteria itself (UNECE returned HTTP 403); the requirement is cited through 49 CFR 173.185.
FCC guidance (KDB) on host-product obligations when using a certified module, and RF-exposure rules for body-worn devices.
A published per-day or per-session price for pre-compliance EMC or electrical-safety testing.
FDA's separate guidance documents on EMC (2022), human factors (2016), ECG electrodes special controls, and the Q-Submission program were identified but not opened.
State law, FTC rules, air-transport battery rules and non-US requirements (EU MDR, radio and battery rules abroad) were out of scope and not researched.
